title: Rachel's Tears and the New Covenant
summary: The LORD promises to bring both Israel and Judah home with singing: the scattered northern tribes will plant vineyards again, the blind and lame will walk on a level road, and Rachel, weeping for her lost children, is told to stop crying because they will return. Then comes the chapter's summit: God will make a new covenant, writing his law on their hearts, so that all will know him, and he will forgive their sins and remember them no more. The chapter ends with God's oath that Israel will endure as long as the sun and stars, and a vision of Jerusalem rebuilt and wholly holy.
story: Chapter 31 is the heart of the Book of Consolation (chapters 30 to 33). Chapter 30 promised healing for an incurable wound; this chapter describes the healed people. Much of the first half speaks to Ephraim, the northern tribes lost to Assyria in 722 BC, so the hope reaches back to include those long given up. The high point, the new covenant of verses 31 to 34, answers the problem the whole book has diagnosed: Israel's heart was stubborn and its sin engraved there (17:1), so a merely restored nation would fail again. God's answer is not a better law but a changed heart. This promise becomes one of the central texts of the New Testament.
historical:
Like chapter 30, this material is undated. Verses addressed to Ephraim and Samaria may come from Jeremiah's early years under Josiah, when there was renewed hope for the north; the whole collection seems to have been gathered around the time of Jerusalem's siege in 588 to 586 BC. Ramah (verse 15) was a town in the territory of Benjamin, about five miles north of Jerusalem. Jeremiah 40:1 says the Babylonians gathered captives there in chains before deporting them, and Jeremiah himself was released there. Rachel, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, was the ancestress of Ephraim (Joseph's son) and Benjamin; 1 Samuel 10:2 places her tomb in Benjamin's territory, though Genesis 35:19 associates it with the road to Bethlehem.

Verses 38 to 40 describe the boundaries of the rebuilt city using landmarks known to Jeremiah's hearers. The Tower of Hananel and the Horse Gate reappear in Nehemiah's account of rebuilding the walls (Nehemiah 3:1, 28), and the Corner Gate is mentioned in 2 Kings 14:13. The hill of Gareb and Goah can no longer be located. The valley of the dead bodies and ashes is almost certainly the Hinnom Valley, where children had been sacrificed and which Jeremiah had called the Valley of Slaughter (7:31-32).
cultural:
The joy of verses 4 to 14 is agricultural and festive: tambourines and dancing, vineyards on the hills of Samaria, pilgrims going up to Zion, grain, new wine, oil, and flocks. Watchmen on the hills of Ephraim calling people to worship in Zion is striking, since northern Israel had worshiped at its own shrines at Bethel and Dan since Jeroboam split from Judah (1 Kings 12:26-33); the divided people will worship together again. Striking the thigh (verse 19) was a gesture of grief or remorse.

The proverb of verse 29, also quoted in Ezekiel 18:2, expressed the exile generation's complaint that they were paying for their ancestors' sins. The image is of the sharp, puckering taste of unripe grapes. Covenants in the ancient Near East were formal agreements, often between a great king and a lesser one, written on tablets and stored in a sacred place. The Sinai covenant was written on stone tablets placed in the ark. A covenant written on hearts would be carried inside each person.
literary: The chapter is a series of poems (verses 1 to 22) followed by prose oracles (23 to 40), several of them beginning with the formula “The days are coming.” The poems move through different speakers and addressees: God to Virgin Israel, a call to the nations, Rachel weeping, Ephraim's confession quoted by God, and God's own yearning (verse 20). Verse 26, “At this I awoke,” suggests that at least some of what precedes came to Jeremiah in a dream or vision. Verse 28 echoes the six verbs of Jeremiah's call (1:10) and the verb “watch” from the almond-branch vision (1:11-12): God watched to tear down and will now watch to build. The new covenant passage (31 to 34) is built on contrast, not like the old covenant, but this, and ends with its ground: “For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.”

outline.t: The great homecoming and the joy of Zion
Rachel weeping, and hope for her children
Building and planting; no more sour grapes
Israel as lasting as creation; the city made holy

doctrines.note: The new covenant keeps the goal of the old, “I will be their God, and they will be My people” (verse 33), but changes the means: God will write his law within, give every member personal knowledge of himself, and forgive sin fully. It is new not because God's law changes but because God changes the people.

The whole promise rests on God's initiative: I will make, I will put, I will inscribe, I will forgive. Forgiveness is the foundation, introduced with “For” in verse 34, and everything else flows from it.

Jeremiah does not mention the Spirit here, but Ezekiel's parallel promise of a new heart links it to God putting his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:26-27), and the New Testament connects the new covenant with the Spirit's work (2 Corinthians 3:3-6).
Verse 20 gives one of the Bible's most tender pictures of God, whose heart yearns for his wayward son and who remembers him even while speaking against him. His love is everlasting (verse 3).

words.note: Berit, covenant, a binding relationship with commitments, sealed by oath. Israel's covenants with God included those with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, and David. Verse 31 is the only place in the Old Testament that uses the exact phrase new covenant.

Chadash, new. It can mean brand new or renewed (the same root gives the word for the new moon). Scholars discuss whether Jeremiah's new covenant is a renewal of Sinai or something fundamentally different; the text says both that it is unlike the covenant their fathers broke and that its content is the same law, now written on the heart.

Chesed, loyal love, steadfast love, or covenant faithfulness (the BSB renders it “loving devotion” in verse 3). It is love that keeps its commitments. God's drawing of his people back rests on this everlasting love.

Salach, to forgive. In the Old Testament this verb always has God as its subject; people pardon each other with other words. Its appearance in verse 34 as the ground of the new covenant shows that the relationship depends on God's own act of forgiveness.

christ: This chapter is quoted in Matthew and Hebrews and stands behind the words of the Last Supper. Matthew 2:17-18 quotes Rachel weeping in Ramah after Herod's slaughter of the children of Bethlehem, seeing Israel's ancient grief over exile repeated at Jesus' birth; Matthew's point is typological, a pattern of sorrow that the coming Savior will answer, as Jeremiah's next verses promise that the children will return. At the Last Supper Jesus took the cup and called it the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), claiming that his death inaugurates what Jeremiah promised. Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes verses 31 to 34 in full, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, to argue that Jesus is the mediator of a better covenant, and it comments that by calling this covenant new God has made the first one obsolete (Hebrews 8:13). Hebrews 10:15-18 returns to the promise that God will remember sins no more, concluding that where there is forgiveness there is no longer any offering for sin. Hebrews quotes from the Greek translation, which in verse 32 reads differently from the Hebrew (where the Hebrew has I was a husband to them, the Greek has God disregarding them), a small reminder that the New Testament writers often used the Greek Bible of their day. Paul calls himself a minister of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:6).

hard.q: The new covenant is promised “with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.” How does it apply to the church, and what does it mean for the Jewish people?
hard.a: Christians agree that Jesus inaugurated the new covenant through his death and that believers from every nation share in its forgiveness and its gift of the Spirit; the Last Supper and Hebrews make this plain. They differ on how the promise to Israel is fulfilled. Many in the Reformed and covenant traditions hold that the church, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, is the renewed Israel to whom the promise now belongs. Dispensational interpreters hold that the church shares in the new covenant's spiritual blessings now, while its national promises to ethnic Israel, including restoration in the land, await future fulfillment. Others take a middle position, drawing on Paul's argument in Romans 9 to 11 that God has not rejected his people and that a future turning of Israel to Christ is expected (Romans 11:26-27 quotes Isaiah and alludes to covenant forgiveness). Verses 35 to 37 make God's commitment to Israel's descendants as fixed as the sun and stars, and every Christian position has to reckon with that oath. This is a second-order question on which faithful Christians disagree, but all should reject contempt for the Jewish people, whom Paul calls beloved for the sake of their forefathers (Romans 11:28).

questions: God's law written on the heart means wanting what God wants, not only knowing it. Where do you see the difference between obeying from outside and from within?
Rachel refuses to be comforted, and God does not rebuke her; he gives her a promise. How does this shape the way we comfort people in grief?
The new covenant ends with God remembering sins no more. How would your life change if you believed that fully about yourself?
